title: List patterns and slices
body: List patterns (C# 11) match sequences by element: `[1, 2, 3]` matches exactly that array, `[first, ..]` captures the first element of a non-empty list, `[.., last]` the last, and `[_, _]` any two-element list. They work on arrays, lists, spans and any type with an indexer and a `Length` or `Count`.

The slice pattern `..` matches zero or more elements and can capture them with a `var` pattern: `[var head, .. var tail]` binds `tail` to the remaining elements (a new array for arrays, a slice for spans). Only one slice pattern is allowed per list pattern.

Elements are patterns themselves, so you can nest: `[> 0, .., < 0]` matches lists that start positive and end negative, and `[string cmd, .. var rest]` is a neat way to parse command-line style input.

List patterns combine well with recursion for teaching: `Sum([]) = 0`, `Sum([var x, .. var rest]) = x + Sum(rest)`. Be aware that capturing the slice of an array allocates each time, so production code over large arrays should use spans or indexes.
Check the empty case first and remember the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis for list patterns is limited; keep a discard arm for inputs you did not anticipate.

question: In `[var first, .. var rest]` applied to an int[], what is rest?
correct: A new array holding every element after the first
wrong: A live view that changes with the original array
reasoning: Slices of arrays are copies; use spans if you need a non-allocating view.
